props.heading: The relationship is the first thing a model can't hold.
props.body: When a student is struggling and frustrated, the thing that keeps them in the room is often a specific human who knows their name, their history, and what kind of encouragement works for them. Claude doesn't have that. It can simulate warmth, but it can't hold a relationship across time in the way a teacher does.

props.heading: The friction law from learning science: there are two kinds of difficulty.
props.body: Unproductive difficulty makes you give up. Productive difficulty — the right kind of struggle — is what builds skill. A model optimized for helpful responses will often resolve the struggle before it becomes productive. A teacher knows when to let the friction stand.

props.heading: The engagement trap: EdTech companies optimize for the metrics that keep users i
props.body: Loved product, weak learning outcomes is the pattern the research keeps finding. AI can produce very high perceived engagement while producing low actual skill transfer. The teacher is the check on that gap.

props.artifactTitle: Claude, Not the Teacher — one card
artifactLines: The relationship: when a student is about to give up, the thing that keeps them going is you — not the platform.
The friction law: remove extraneous load (logistics, confusion). Protect germane load (the struggle that is the learning).
The split: drafting is machine-shaped. The parent call, the room read, the which-student-gets-what — those are yours alone.
Loved isn't learned: engagement is not instruction. The tool optimized for clicks removed the friction that builds judgment.
AI did: draft content, generate options · you do: carry the relationship · support fades at: the moment AI is put between teacher and student
